The training matrix provided outlines several mandatory training requirements, including those designated as "priority" for supervisors. However, it was found that some of these supervisor-specific trainings were not executed as planned. Additionally, the current training delivery is being conducted by the HSE Manager and HSE Coordinator, neither of whom have completed a formal "Train the Trainer" course. Furthermore, electrical-related training is being facilitated by the HSE Manager, who is not certified or competent to deliver such specialized instruction. These gaps raise concerns about the effectiveness, compliance, and credibility of the training program.

Two audits were conducted by the HSE team from other Abyatona projects. However, no audit schedule was provided, and there was no documentation of the audit reports or the criteria used during the audits. Additionally, there was no evidence that the audit findings or outcomes were communicated to the project team. This lack of transparency and documentation undermines the effectiveness of the audit process and limits the project's ability to implement corrective actions or improvements based on the audit results.

However, upon reviewing the HSE observation data for August and September, it is evident that the most frequently reported observation did not show significant improvement. Although a strategic plan was applied during the same period to address this issue, the lack of measurable progress suggests that the observations were not adequately monitored or evaluated to identify the root cause. As a result, an effective system to drive improvement was not successfully implemented.

The last two incidents—one involving first aid and the other a near miss—were investigated and documented in Enablon, with all relevant recommendations provided. However, no lessons learned were developed or shared as part of the incident closure process. Additionally, there is no evidence that these incidents were communicated to the workforce. This lack of dissemination limits the opportunity for organizational learning and may hinder efforts to prevent recurrence.

There was evidence that the lessons learned shared by Oxagon Projects were discussed during toolbox meetings, indicating some level of knowledge transfer and engagement. However, these lessons were not posted on the HSE bulletin board or in worker shelters. This limits broader visibility and reinforcement of key safety messages among the workforce, reducing the potential impact of shared learnings across all site personnel.

The Contractor reports that all HSSE-related non-conformities (NCRs) have been closed. In the culvert ABCD area, a scaffolding structure approximately 5 meters in height was installed to access the top level of the culvert. However, no assessment or documented rescue plan was found to address potential emergencies related to working at height, which poses a serious safety risk. Additionally, surface repair activities inside the culvert required adequate lighting to ensure visibility, yet no lighting system was provided. As a result, workers were compelled to remove their safety glasses to see their tasks clearly, compromising their eye protection and overall safety. Immediate corrective actions are recommended to address both the rescue planning and lighting deficiencies.

Furthermore, there is no structured training tracking system in use, and workers have not been issued training cards or identification stickers to verify their participation and competency.

Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) non-compliance was observed on site:

Several workers were found wearing damaged safety shoes, compromising foot protection.

Some workers lacked clear safety glasses, which are essential for visibility and eye protection in low-light or indoor environments.

A few supervisors were seen wearing fashion glasses instead of certified safety glasses, failing to meet PPE standards.

These deficiencies pose significant safety risks and indicate a lack of enforcement and awareness regarding PPE requirements. Immediate corrective actions, including PPE inspections, replacements, and reinforcement of compliance through supervision and training, are strongly recommended.

Several cases of wounds and inflammation among workers were reported and treated on-site through basic wound cleaning procedures. However, there is no documented evidence confirming the proper disposal of the resulting medical waste. Specifically, no waste manifest reports were available from either the waste collector or the receiving facility.

Tripping hazards were identified within the culvert (ABCD) and along the scaffolding access routes. Numerous rocks and scattered construction materials were observed obstructing the walkways, posing a risk to personnel movement and potentially leading to slips, trips, or falls.

A kidney stone complaint and wound/imflammation were recorded in the clinic register; however, this case was not communicated to site management for further assessment or follow-up action and investigation.

Surface repair work is being conducted inside the culvert under inadequate lighting conditions. It was observed that workers were removing their safety glasses to perform tasks, likely due to poor visibility.
Four portable toilets were found to be emitting strong odors and were in a visibly unhygienic condition

Such incidents should be addressed promptly to reinforce compliance and prevent potential risks.

The HSE plan identifies ‘zero accident’ as the overall objective; however, it lacks detailed performance targets and measurable KPIs to monitor progress. The plan should include monthly or quarterly targets for both leading and lagging indicators—such as TRIR, LTIFR, number of NCRs, near‑miss reporting, closure rate of observations, management walkthrough frequency, and other proactive HSE activities. Additionally, a clear strategy outlining how these targets will be achieved is required to ensure effective implementation and performance monitoring.

Roles and responsibilities have been reviewed in the Contractor’s HSE Plan (03‑189038‑4200000029‑NBC‑HSE‑PLN‑000001_03, Section 7.3). However, the plan does not include a detailed program describing how the contractor will ensure that each key position understands and accepts their health and safety roles and responsibilities prior to engaging in site activities. Additionally, the contractor has not established a program or mechanism to evaluate whether each position effectively delivers their assigned roles and responsibilities (i.e., performance evaluation).

Upon review, it was noted that the contractor has not established a formal training program to guide the management of training requirements for the project. There is no assigned trainer for the project, and all training has been conducted solely by the HSE Manager. In addition, the training matrix indicates that a Surveyor is required to attend “Scaffolding Training,” which does not align with the Surveyor’s actual work scope. This demonstrates that the training program was not properly developed or tailored for the earthworks project, leading to inaccurate and inappropriate training assignments. 03-189038-4200000029-NBC-HSE-PLN-000001_03, section 12

The contractor does not have a comprehensive plan or program for conducting audits and inspections. No schedule has been provided for their planned audits. In addition, plant and equipment inspection monitoring is not being practiced. One example observed was a smoke detector that had no inspection record. Furthermore, two exhaust fans in the toilets of both site offices were found with improperly spliced electrical cables. These issues indicate inadequate implementation and control of the contractor’s audit and inspection processes.

The HSE data currently being monitored and evaluated is limited to safety observations, which are reviewed on a monthly basis. The contractor provides the top three highest‑rated safety observations along with an associated improvement plan. However, there is no program or mechanism in place to measure the effectiveness of the implemented improvement plan. Document reviewed - SR1-NBC-029-KPI Jan-2026

The contractor’s aim and vision have been provided which is zero accident in the approved HSE Plan and within the Contractor’s HSE Policy. However, the HSSE objectives, targets, implementation strategy, and processes for measuring effective implementation are not clearly demonstrated based on the evidence submitted.
For example, there are no defined HSSE targets, no audit schedule, and no measurable indicators such as the required number of near-miss reports, among others.

There is no evidence provided to demonstrate that the contractor has an established program to ensure that employees understand and acknowledge their roles and responsibilities related to health and safety.
Additionally, there is no documented process or program showing how the contractor ensures that each individual consistently fulfills their assigned HSSE roles and responsibilities during daily site operations.

Training Plan Classification:
The training plan is still in Code C, indicating that it is incomplete or not fully developed.
Lack of Training Needs Analysis (TNA):
There is no evidence demonstrating that a training needs analysis was conducted prior to developing the training matrix. As a result, the matrix does not clearly reflect competency requirements aligned with job roles.
No Systematic Approach to Address Language Barriers:
The contractor has not provided a structured method to manage or overcome language barriers, which may affect effective training delivery and employee comprehension

The contractor compiles safety observations on a monthly basis and analyzes them to determine actions for improving that month’s performance. These reports are submitted to the Oxagon HSE Department as part of the KPI reporting system.
However, there is no evidence that the contractor evaluates the effectiveness of the corrective actions taken in the previous month. Additionally, there is no demonstration of senior management involvement in reviewing or evaluating site performance.
It was found that only one person is reporting in Enablon.

Recent medical treatment case review identified the following gaps:
No formal investigation methodology (e.g., TapRooT, Fishbone) was applied.
HSE team members involved in the investigation are not trained in incident investigation techniques.
Identified causes were not aligned with the recommended corrective actions.
No Lessons Learned document was developed following the incident.

The contractor provided evidence that HSSE information—such as lessons learned and safety campaigns—has been communicated to the workforce. However, no lessons learned were developed for the recent medical treatment case, and therefore it was not communicated from leadership down to the worker level.
This gap demonstrates the absence of a robust HSSE communication process, particularly in relation to incident learning and organizational feedback mechanisms.

The contractor has not initiated any formal HSSE communication programs within their organization. For example, there is no evidence of HSE meetings, steering committee meetings, or other structured communication forums being conducted.

One NCR related to VVS (PWAS) was issued; however, it was not communicated to the supervision level, preventing lessons learned from being shared across the organization. This indicates that the contractor must develop an effective communication and escalation process to ensure that all relevant information and required actions are properly conveyed—from senior management down to the worker level—so that lessons associated with each NCR are understood and procedural violations are fully recognized.
Furthermore, roles and responsibilities must be clearly defined from senior positions down to line supervisors to support accountability, ensure proper escalation, and enable consistent implementation of corrective actions.

The contractor provided evidence that a reward and recognition program is being implemented on site. However, the criteria specified in the Contractor’s HSE Plan are not being followed, indicating a gap between the documented requirements and the actual implementation.

The contractor has not initiated any formal HSSE communication programs within their organization. For example, there is no evidence of HSE meetings, steering committee meetings, or other structured communication forums being conducted.

A review of the contractor’s previous performance shows that a Non‑Conformance Report (NCR) was issued related to the Vehicle Verification Program (no PWAS in place). Additionally, several workers were found to be in violation of employment requirements (freelance workers).
These issues demonstrate significant gaps in the contractor’s pre‑mobilization process, indicating that the required verification, compliance checks, and approval steps were not effectively implemented prior to deploying personnel and equipment to the site.
The first internal audit is scheduled to commence in Q1 of 2026.

Based on the evidence provided, there is no established schedule for leadership tours. Additionally, the evidence from recent walkthrough activities indicates a lack of participation from senior management, demonstrating limited leadership engagement in site HSSE oversight.

* Planning for HS activities is generally limited to the OXAGON Projects’ HS activities (Monthly Engagement Schedule).
* No internal, project level goals, measures or targets (other than zero accidents).
* No integration of the OXAGON Projects “Contractor Senior Management Engagement” targets.

* The relationship and respective roles and responsibilities between corporate and regional management and project management are not defined.
* Management and supervisory positions do not have documented responsibilities that clearly outline their health and safety obligations, including requirements for the design, implementation, or governance of the health and safety system.
* Roles with management or supervisory duties show no documented evidence that they receive clear instructions outlining their individual health and safety responsibilities.
* The organization cannot show documented evidence that the performance of managers and supervisors is assessed against their specific health and safety responsibilities.

* Audit and Inspection Plan findings:
(a). Schedule provides no focus on critical risks or critical control systems (e.g. PTW, RAMS)
(b) No inspection or audit tools specified.
(c) No requirements for evaluating the implementation of the plan specified.

* Inspection targets are too low (e.g. 1 critical risk control inspection per month).
* No integration of the OXAGON Projects “Contractor Senior Management Engagement” targets.
* Supervisors not conducting the mandated daily inspections.
* Only two HSE personnel (HSE Manager and HSE Coordinator) are utilizing Enablon.

* The incident‑management section of the Project Health and Safety Management Plan is poorly structured, lacks a clear, sequential process flow, and omits several critical steps, including securing the incident scene, collecting evidence, and appointing a competent investigator and investigation team.
* No evidence available that demonstrates the competency of the incident investigators.

* No charter or procedure outlining the meeting’s purpose, objectives, participants (including corporate or regional management), and operating schedule and rules.
* Issues for discussion and resolution are not dealt with in a strategic manner i.e. no evidence of investigation or analysis to identify underlying causes and development of measures to prevent reoccurrence.
* No reporting on the implementation or outcomes of the Monthly Engagement Schedule.
* No review of performance against the OXAGON Projects leading and lagging indicators.
* No review of previous documented decisions to verify action implementation and effectiveness.
Other findings in Communications:
* No evidence to demonstrate that project HSE performance is communicated to the workforce.
 * Supervisors are typically Arabic speaking. Evidence indicates that this compromises the supervisor’s ability to effectively :
* Understand and comprehend instructions written in English (some translation of documents has occurred, mainly RAMS).
* Communicate / brief workers under their control who are predominantly Hindi / Urdu speakers.
* Limited evidence that information relating to incidents (injuries, NCRs, performance management issues, etc.) are communicated to the site workers.

* No evidence of a documented performance management process.
* Warning letters are being issued to workers and supervisors without defining the criteria relating to the non-conformance or less-than-adequate performance.

* No evidence of corporate or regional management participation in mandated activities.
* Specified site leadership involvement in site walkthrough not evident.

• In reviewing the Consortium HSE Plan, the vision and aims is limited to zero accident; however, there are no HSSE targets established for the last quarter.
• This indicates that the consortium lacks a clear HSSE performance direction, as measurable targets are essential for monitoring progress, driving improvement, and ensuring accountability.
• Additionally, during the last quarterly consortium meeting with senior management, there was no discussion on HSSE performance review or HSSE look ahead targets.

• In reviewing the roles and responsibilities and the process for employee acknowledgment, Archirodon provided clear evidence of a structured process ensuring that each member of the leadership and supervisory team understands and accepts their HSE roles and responsibilities.
• On the other hand, DEME presented a different process, focused primarily on general employee roles and responsibilities, where HSE responsibilities were not clearly defined or emphasized. While both companies have employee performance evaluation systems, their approaches differ significantly.
• This demonstrates that the two companies are using different systems to deliver HSE performance review, which does not reflect a unified consortium performance expectation. As a consortium, a consistent and aligned approach is required to ensure that HSE responsibilities, performance reviews, and accountability mechanisms are applied uniformly across all entities.

• During the review of the consortium’s training documents and implementation, the provided training matrix clearly identified the required training courses for each position. However, upon verification of the required training for the Construction Manager position, it was found that only five trainings had been completed, whereas the matrix indicates that ten training topics are required for this role.
• When asked whether there was evidence of a training plan covering the remaining required training for the Construction Manager, no training plan or schedule was provided. This demonstrates a gap in ensuring compliance with consortium training requirements and indicates that the training program is not being effectively implemented or monitored.
• There is no dedicated resource for the management of training for the consortium level.

• Specific plan/schedule for audit and inspection.
• Analysis of audit and inspections findings to inform future improvement strategies.
• In the review of the internal audit evidence, Archirodon provided documentation demonstrating a clear hierarchy of information flow, from management level down to site leadership, ensuring that required actions are communicated and implemented. Additionally, Archirodon’s audit included a notified observation categorized as “Needs Improvement” for one identified area, showing evidence of follow up and corrective action tracking.
• On the other hand, DEME provided evidence of an internal audit conducted mid last year; however, there is no evidence that the audit report was communicated to senior management. This indicates a gap in the escalation process and weakens leadership oversight of audit findings and required corrective actions.
• Since the project operates as a consortium, the internal audit process should be harmonized across both companies, applying one unified audit criterion, with a consistent reporting, communication, and follow up mechanism. Conducting internal audits in isolation, with different processes and communication methods, does not reflect a cohesive consortium level management system, and may result in inconsistent application of corrective actions and performance expectations.

• There is evidence that monthly safety observations are being collected and evaluated, with documented improvement actions. This report forms part of the monthly KPI submission sent to the client.
• However, no evidence was provided to demonstrate that the improvement actions were measured for effectiveness or that they resulted in significant, sustained performance improvement. The absence of such verification indicates a gap in closing the feedback loop and ensuring continual improvement.
• Observer performance, compliance system requirements, identifying trends in performance and developing improvement strategies.
• Additionally, the presentation slide from the previous consortium senior management meeting did not include any information regarding observation trends, improvement actions, or performance evaluation. This suggests that observation outcomes and improvement measures are not being escalated to senior management, limiting strategic oversight and decision making.
